description: LunarSiteNav is a web tool for comparing lunar landing sites and dates. For each site it draws the real terrain horizon from NASA LRO LOLA topography out to 200 km and places the Sun and Earth on it hourly via JPL Horizons API. It shows sunlight (power), Earth view (direct comms), time to sunset or Earthset, and changes over 92 days. Up to three sites compare side by side; one click shows a 14-day launch slip. South-pole trade-off: Shackleton rim stays sunlit but loses Earth up to 13 days.
summary: LunarSiteNav is a web tool that lets mission planners, educators and the public compare lunar landing sites and dates at a glance. For each site it draws the real terrain horizon, computed from NASA LRO LOLA topography out to 200 km, and places the Sun and Earth on it hour by hour using the NASA JPL Horizons API. From that it tells you whether the site is sunlit (power) and whether Earth is in view (direct-to-Earth communication), how long until sunset or Earthset, and how both change over the next 92 days. Up to three sites sit side by side as colour-coded timelines with a comparison table, and one click shows what a 14-day launch slip does. The tool makes the south-pole trade-off obvious: our Shackleton rim point stays sunlit for the whole period but loses Earth for up to 13 days at a time, while near-side polar sites keep Earth in view but face two-week nights.
details:
What it does

Planning a landing near the Moon's south pole means balancing sunlight for power against a line of sight to Earth for communication, and both depend on local terrain and the date. Existing tools (QuickMap, Moon Trek, JPL Horizons) hold the data but are built for detailed analysis. LunarSiteNav puts the answer on one screen.

·       Horizon panorama: a 360 degree view of the terrain horizon with the Sun and Earth at the chosen hour, their paths for the next 14 days, and live status chips (sunlit or shadow, Earth in view or hidden, time to the next sunset, sunrise, Earthset or Earthrise). The vertical scale is stretched so polar angles of one or two degrees are readable.

·       Date flexibility: an hourly slider across 92 days and buttons for -7, -1, +1 and +7 days and a 14-day launch slip.

·       Side-by-side comparison: up to three sites as 92-day colour strips (Sun and Earth, Sun only, Earth only, neither) and a table with percent sunlit, percent Earth in view, percent both, longest darkness, longest Earth blackout, the current Sun and Earth elevation against the terrain behind them, the longest Sun-plus-Earth window from the chosen date, and site elevation.

·       Curated sites: Apollo 11 (equatorial reference), Chandrayaan-3 Vikram (ISRO), IM-1 Odysseus (NASA CLPS), the Malapert massif and the Shackleton crater rim area; any coordinates can be added.

Results (14 Nov 2026 to 14 Feb 2027, hourly)

Apollo 11: 51% sunlit, Earth always in view, longest night 356 h. Chandrayaan-3: 51%, Earth always, 364 h. IM-1: 45%, Earth always, 379 h. Malapert (representative point): 61%, Earth always, 321 h. Shackleton rim (representative point): 100% sunlit, Earth in view 54%, longest Earth blackout 322 h (about 13 days). A site that solves power can break communication, and the tool shows it in seconds.

How it works

·       scripts/build_dataset.py calls the JPL Horizons API for each site with the observer on the Moon (CENTER = coord@301, geodetic coordinates) and requests apparent azimuth and elevation of the Sun (10) and Earth (399) every hour for 92 days.

·       The same script reads NASA LRO LOLA gridded topography (LDEM_16, 16 pixels per degree, about 1.9 km) from the PDS Geosciences Node and, for each degree of azimuth, marches along a great circle from 1 to 200 km, samples elevation bilinearly and computes the elevation angle of every terrain point including the curvature of a 1737.4 km Moon, keeping the maximum. That is the terrain horizon for an observer on a 2 m mast.

·       A body counts as visible when its elevation is above the terrain horizon at its azimuth. The Moon has no atmosphere, so no refraction correction is needed.

·       The front end (HTML, CSS, JavaScript, SVG, no libraries) loads the precomputed data, so it works offline and fast, and every state is a shareable URL.

Benefits

·       Engineers can re-evaluate alternative sites and dates in seconds when launch dates move.

·       Educators and the public can see why the lunar south pole is both attractive and hard.

·       The method is transparent and reproducible from public NASA data with one script.

Limits and next steps

The 1.9 km terrain grid misses small nearby hills, so sunlit fractions are upper bounds; final decisions should use high-resolution LOLA products, QuickMap or Moon Trek. Next steps: higher-resolution polar DEM tiles around selected sites, solar-array power estimates for mast heights, relay-satellite coverage and an in-browser custom-site mode.

Tools

Python 3 with numpy; JPL Horizons API; LRO LOLA data from PDS; JavaScript, HTML, CSS, SVG; GitHub Pages; Playwright and ffmpeg for the demo video; Kokoro TTS for narration.
